Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

AURORA, Colorado (CNN) -- The Atlanta lawyer with tuberculosis who caused an international health scare after traveling to Europe and back underwent surgery Tuesday to remove the diseased portion of one of his lungs. TB patient Andrew Speaker set off an international health scare when he traveled to Europe for his wedding in May. Andrew Speaker, 31, had the roughly two-hour operation to remove the upper lobe of his right lung at the University of Colorado Hospital. He's been under treatment at National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver since the end of May. CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta, who observed the surgery for about an hour, explained that the unusual procedure consisted of inserting a video camera in a tube in one small incision in the right side of Speaker's chest, and putting instruments through another incision. When the infected portion of the lung was cut out, it was placed inside a bag while still inside the attorney's chest cavity and the bag was sealed inside a tube before being removed. The main reason for sealing the infected tissue was to prevent it from re-infecting Speaker as it was removed, Gupta said after the operation. Doctors also wanted to make sure they didn't "release any of that tuberculosis bacteria into the operating room, into the rest of the hospital," Gupta said before the surgery on CNN's "American Morning." Watch Andrew Speaker discuss his reasons for having surgery with CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta » . Doctors said the operation went well and there was not much bleeding, Gupta said. The portion of the lung that was removed showed the effects of the disease, Gupta said. "A regular lung is very pink with a smooth, glistening surface," he said. "This had a lot of bumps on it, and the areas that were diseased were very dark with white nodules." Speaker will most likely recover at the University of Colorado Hospital for another couple of days, and will return to National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver to finish his antibiotic course. He will still have to continue taking the medications prescribed by his doctors to fight the tuberculosis until cultures taken from him are negative for tuberculosis bacteria for eight weeks. At that point, he will be considered non-infectious, but he will still be monitored by health care professionals. Speaker said it was his decision to have the surgery, which is just one of his treatment options. "With the amount of treatment I'm going to be on, the doctors said if you go ahead and have this surgery, you don't have to worry 10 years from now, or 20 years from now, or 30 years from now if it's ever going to come back, so it's worth the peace of mind to me," the attorney said. Speaker was originally found to have an extremely drug resistant strain (XDR-TB) of the respiratory disease earlier this year, but on July 3 doctors said he had multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), which is treatable with less toxic drugs. Speaker and his fiancee had gone to Europe on May 12 for their wedding in Greece, despite warnings from the Fulton County Health Department in Georgia that he should not fly because he risked infecting fellow passengers. Since then, eight people who shared a flight with Speaker have filed a lawsuit against him, seeking $1.3 million in damages. Rosalind Yee -- an attorney for the plaintiffs who said her clients include a ninth person related to one of the passengers but who was not on the flight -- said all eight passengers have undergone TB tests since they returned home. One of them, a 72-year-old man, tested positive for TB on a skin test, though it was not clear that Speaker was the source. The man's X-rays were normal, she said, and he is awaiting results of further tests. In the past year, there have been about 124 cases of MDR-TB in the United States. About half of those patients have elected to undergo the surgery to remove the diseased portion of their lungs, Gupta said. E-mail to a friend .

Speaker, 31, underwent the approximately two-hour procedure at the University of Colorado Hospital. He had been receiving care at Denver’s National Jewish Medical and Research Center since late May.

CNN medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta watched about an hour of the operation. He said surgeons used an uncommon technique involving two small openings in the right side of Speaker’s chest. A tube containing a video camera was inserted through one opening, while surgical tools were passed through the other.

After doctors cut away the infected lung tissue, they enclosed it in a bag while it was still within Speaker’s chest. The bag was then sealed inside a tube and extracted. Gupta said this precaution was primarily intended to keep the tissue from infecting Speaker again during removal. Before the procedure, he told CNN’s “American Morning” that doctors also wanted to avoid allowing any tuberculosis bacteria to escape into the operating room or elsewhere in the hospital.

Gupta reported that the surgery was successful and involved little bleeding. The removed tissue visibly reflected the damage caused by tuberculosis. He described a healthy lung as pink, smooth and shiny, whereas Speaker’s diseased tissue had numerous bumps, darkened areas and white nodules.

Speaker was expected to remain at the University of Colorado Hospital for several more days before returning to National Jewish Medical and Research Center to complete his antibiotic regimen. He must continue taking the prescribed tuberculosis drugs until cultures remain free of TB bacteria for eight weeks. He will then be classified as no longer infectious, although medical professionals will continue to monitor him.

The operation was one of several possible treatments, and Speaker said he personally chose to undergo it. He explained that doctors told him surgery, combined with his extensive treatment, could eliminate concerns that the disease might return 10, 20 or 30 years later. He said that reassurance made the procedure worthwhile.

Earlier in the year, Speaker was initially diagnosed with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis, known as XDR-TB. On July 3, however, physicians announced that he instead had multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, or MDR-TB, which can be treated using medications that are less toxic.

Despite being advised by Georgia’s Fulton County Health Department not to fly because he could infect other travelers, Speaker and his fiancée left for Europe on May 12 to be married in Greece. Their trip triggered the international health scare.

Eight passengers who were aboard a flight with Speaker later sued him, requesting $1.3 million in damages. Their attorney, Rosalind Yee, said her clients also included a ninth person who was related to one passenger but had not been on the plane.

According to Yee, all eight passengers received tuberculosis testing after returning home. A skin test was positive in one case involving a 72-year-old man, although it remained uncertain whether Speaker had infected him. Yee said the man’s X-rays were normal and that he was waiting for additional test results.

Approximately 124 MDR-TB cases had been recorded in the United States during the previous year. Gupta said roughly half of those patients chose surgery to remove the infected sections of their lungs.

counterfactuals.output:
## TB traveler undergoes lung surgery as airline passengers pursue lawsuit

**DENVER —** Andrew Speaker, the Atlanta attorney whose international travel while infected with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis triggered a global health alert in 2007, underwent a roughly two-hour operation to remove the most severely damaged portion of his right lung.

Surgeons removed the upper lobe, where doctors believed most of the infection was concentrated. The procedure was intended to reduce the number of tuberculosis bacteria in Speaker’s body and improve the chances that a prolonged course of antibiotics would eradicate the remaining infection.

Doctors reported that the operation went as planned. Speaker was expected to remain hospitalized for several days before continuing treatment under close supervision.

### Surgery added to lengthy drug regimen

Removing part of a lung is not standard treatment for most tuberculosis patients. TB is generally treated with a combination of antibiotics, but surgery can be considered when the infection is concentrated in one area and the bacteria are resistant to the most effective first-line drugs.

Speaker had been diagnosed with **multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, or MDR-TB**, meaning the strain was resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two principal TB medications. Early testing led federal officials to describe the strain as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR-TB, but subsequent laboratory analysis showed that it did not meet the full XDR definition and it was reclassified as MDR-TB.

Even after the operation, Speaker faced many months of treatment with several second-line drugs. Such medications can be less effective, more toxic and more difficult to tolerate than standard TB therapy. MDR-TB treatment commonly lasts 18 months or longer, with doctors repeatedly testing sputum samples to determine whether a patient remains infectious and whether the bacteria are responding.

The surgery did not, by itself, cure Speaker. Its purpose was to remove the section of lung containing the heaviest concentration of disease while antibiotics attacked bacteria elsewhere in his body.

### International trip set off public-health alarm

The case drew worldwide attention after Speaker traveled to Europe for his wedding despite having been told that he had a drug-resistant form of tuberculosis.

He left the United States aboard an Air France flight from Atlanta to Paris and later traveled through Europe. After federal health officials contacted him overseas and warned him not to take a commercial flight, Speaker returned to North America on a Czech Airlines flight from Prague to Montreal. He and his wife then drove across the Canadian border into the United States.

Speaker was subsequently placed under a federal isolation order—the first such federal action involving a U.S. citizen in decades—and transported to specialized medical facilities for evaluation and treatment.

Speaker maintained that, before leaving for Europe, he had not been expressly ordered to remain in the United States and did not believe he posed a substantial risk to others. Public-health officials disputed parts of his account, saying he had been warned against commercial travel.

The controversy prompted scrutiny of communication among Speaker, his physicians and government agencies, as well as questions about why border authorities did not stop him despite an alert.

### Passengers allege negligent exposure

Passengers who shared the Prague-to-Montreal flight later filed a lawsuit accusing Speaker of knowingly exposing them to a potentially deadly infectious disease.

The complaint sought damages and medical-monitoring costs and was presented as a proposed class action on behalf of passengers who said they had been forced to undergo testing and live with anxiety about possible infection. The plaintiffs alleged negligence and emotional distress, arguing that Speaker boarded the flight after receiving warnings from health authorities.

Those claims were allegations, not findings of liability. To prevail, the passengers would have had to establish that Speaker breached a legal duty and caused a compensable injury. The absence of a confirmed TB infection among the plaintiffs could complicate claims for conventional physical-injury damages, although they also sought compensation for testing expenses and fear of developing the disease.

Health officials emphasized that tuberculosis is not spread as easily as common respiratory viruses. Transmission generally requires prolonged exposure to airborne bacteria released when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, speaks or sings. The greatest concern centered on passengers seated near Speaker during the long flight.

Speaker was described as having relatively limited symptoms, and later investigations did not establish that he had transmitted tuberculosis to fellow travelers. Passengers and crew members considered potentially exposed were nevertheless urged to receive an initial TB test and follow-up testing several weeks later because infection may not be detectable immediately.

The episode became a prominent example of the tension between individual freedom and public-health authority, while Speaker’s surgery underscored the complexity of treating tuberculosis that no longer responds to the most powerful standard drugs.
